query: Consider the following context: The combination of elevated temperature and tribo-corrosion leads to the accelerated degradation of structural components used in many extreme environments. Recently developed high-entropy alloys (HEAs) with multiple principal elements have the potential for superior degradation resistance compared with presently used structural alloys. In that context, which material can be used for superior tribo-corrosion degradation resistance, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A powder‐metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 high‐entropy alloy will show superior tribo‐corrosion degradation resistance at elevated temperatures because its tribo-oxidation under dynamic wear conditions promotes the in situ formation of a dense, protective spinel-type oxide film that minimizes direct metal/solution contact.
generation.material_initial_state: AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 high-entropy alloy fabricated by inert gas atomization followed by spark plasma sintering, exhibiting a multiphase microstructure including B2 and A2 phases and minor secondary phases.
generation.intervention: Expose the alloy to reciprocating wear under elevated temperatures (e.g., 800–900 °C) in a corrosive environment using an Al2O3 counterbody.
generation.conditions: High-temperature (800–900 °C) reciprocating wear tests in air (or a controlled corrosive medium such as a NaCl environment) with constant load and frequency conditions similar to those in tribo-corrosion testing.
generation.structural_mediator: In situ formation of a continuous, adherent spinel-type oxide layer during tribo-oxidation that acts as a barrier against corrosion and wear.
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, the high-entropy alloy undergoes tribo-oxidation; the reactive constituent elements form a protective spinel oxide, which reduces the direct exposure of the metal surface to the corrosive environment and minimizes wear, thereby enhancing tribo-corrosion resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to its performance at lower temperatures, the alloy will achieve lower wear depths and reduced coefficients of friction, indicating an improvement in tribo-corrosion resistance due to the formation of the protective oxide film.
generation.baseline: At lower temperatures (e.g., room temperature to 500 °C), limited oxide film formation leads to higher wear rates and greater corrosion susceptibility.
generation.boundary: This enhanced performance is expected only under conditions where dynamic wear and elevated temperatures coexist; performance in environments lacking sufficient thermal activation for oxide formation remains uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: The long-term durability and adhesion of the oxide film under fluctuating loads and varying corrosive species, as well as its stability under sustained cyclic conditions, remain to be conclusively determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform reciprocating tribo-corrosion tests on samples of the AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 high-entropy alloy at various temperatures (e.g., room temperature, 500 °C, 800 °C, and 900 °C) in a controlled corrosive environment using a standardized load and Al2O3 counterbody. Assess wear depth, coefficient of friction, and oxide layer formation via XRD and SEM after testing.
measurements: Thickness and phase identification of oxide layers (via XRD and SEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, at elevated temperatures (800–900 °C), the alloy does not exhibit a significant reduction in wear depth and friction compared to low-temperature tests, or if no dense protective spinel-type oxide layer is observed, the hypothesis will be falsified.

System: Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy (HEA).
